ios.desc:
Atrophy is a short diagnostic that measures how much of your judgment you've handed to LLMs.

It runs entirely offline. No accounts, no servers, no analytics, no third-party SDKs. Everything stays on your device.

WHAT IT DOES
- A focused calibration quiz: spot AI slop, verify weak claims, explain back what you read, gauge confidence.
- A calibration score with a plain-language reading of where you're solid and where you're drifting.
- A shareable result card you can save to Photos.

WHAT IT DOESN'T DO
- No tracking. No advertising IDs. No ATT prompt — there's nothing to track.
- No content rented from a server. The drills ship in the app.
- No social graph, no leaderboard, no streaks.

ATROPHY PRO (Optional Subscription)
Unlocks the Practice Pack — additional drills for ongoing calibration.
- Monthly: $4.99 / month
- Annual: $49.99 / year

Subscriptions auto-renew until canceled. Cancel anytime in your Apple ID settings (Settings → Apple ID → Subscriptions). Account is charged for renewal within 24 hours prior to the end of the current period. Payment is charged to your Apple ID account at confirmation of purchase.

Privacy policy: https://atrophy-ai.github.io/privacy.html
Terms of use: https://atrophy-ai.github.io/terms.html

show_hn.title: Show HN: I made an iOS app to gauge AI over-reliance and AI psychosis

quotes.text:
Atrophy is an iOS self-report quiz aimed at software engineers who use LLMs heavily enough at work to wonder if they're trending toward AI over-reliance or some form of AI psychosis.

I built it because I noticed a pattern: formerly AI-skeptical coworkers now open every standup or design discussion with "I asked Claude..." or "Claude told me..." for technical problems and design decisions. I've felt the same pull myself to delegate every task or problem to AI. It's easy to lean on these tools for almost any amount of critical thinking or problem solving, and I'm worried about what it means when knowledge workers atrophy their cognition this way.

I'm not anti-AI nor do I think these models will completely replace software engineers. But as long as humans are still in the loop for software engineering, I don't have a good answer for how to avoid becoming overly reliant on these models. How do we gauge how over-reliant we've become, or maintain responsibility for the programs and systems we ship while outsourcing 90% of the judgment we used to be required to make? How do we learn what good code looks like when PR size and velocity have grown to the point that only the important parts get reviewed?

I'm hoping to work on better ways to notice this pattern and practice our way back from it. This is my first attempt (offline only, no accounts/analytics).
